Frederick the Great. Also known as Frederick the Second, the King of Prussia who transformed it into a major European power through military genius and enlightened absolutism. His victories in the War of Austrian Succession and the Seven Years' War established Prussia as a rival to Austria and Russia, making him one of history's most influential military and political figures.

Born in seventeen twelve, Frederick inherited a strong Prussian military and a moderately developed state at age twenty-eight, then vastly expanded both through aggressive foreign policy and administrative reform. He won the War of Austrian Succession from seventeen forty to seventeen forty-eight, seizing the wealthy province of Silesia from Austria and doubling Prussia's territory and resources, establishing Prussia as a major power. His invasion of Silesia in seventeen forty launched a series of wars that reshaped European power dynamics and established Prussia as a rival to Austria's traditional dominance. Frederick engaged in the costly Seven Years' War from seventeen fifty-six to seventeen sixty-three against a coalition of Austria, Russia, and Saxony; despite near-defeat when surrounded and nearly bankrupt, he secured Prussian gains and status. The war's end elevated Prussia to great-power status and demonstrated Frederick's strategic brilliance in surviving near-impossible odds through mobile warfare and concentration of force. He embodied enlightened absolutism, reforming the Prussian bureaucracy with meritocratic principles, tolerating religious minorities including Catholics and Jews, and establishing efficient administrative practices. He corresponded extensively with Voltaire and cultivated French Enlightenment ideas, presenting himself as a philosopher-king despite his ruthless militarism and autocratic rule. Frederick created a small standing army of approximately two hundred thousand men of unprecedented efficiency and discipline, innovating tactics and organization that influenced European warfare for generations. He established Prussia as an intellectual center, founding academies and inviting scholars, while pursuing aggressive territorial expansion through military conquest and diplomacy. He was a contemporary rival to Catherine the Great of Russia; together they dominated Eastern European politics in the late eighteenth century, partitioning Poland between them. Frederick the Great connects to the Prussian Empire as the state he transformed into a major power; the House of Hohenzollern as his royal house, which he elevated to dynastic prominence; Catherine the Second as contemporary Russian empress and occasional ally, often rival; the Enlightenment as the philosophical movement he claimed to embody; the War of Austrian Succession as his first major conquest, establishing his reputation; the Seven Years' War as his greatest trial and ultimate validation as a military genius; and Voltaire as French philosopher with whom he maintained correspondence.
